after: @classmethod gives the method the class used for the call. Its first argument is usually named cls. A factory method creates and returns a new object. Here, from_minutes returns cls("Study", minutes), so cls decides which class to create.

@staticmethod receives only the arguments you pass. Here, valid_minutes receives minutes and returns whether it is zero or more. Python does not add self or cls. This method checks a number. It does not change existing sessions or automatically check their minutes.

```python
class Session:
    def __init__(self, title, minutes):
        self.title = title
        self.minutes = minutes

    @classmethod
    def from_minutes(cls, minutes):
        return cls("Study", minutes)

    @staticmethod
    def valid_minutes(minutes):
        return minutes >= 0

class SpecialSession(Session):
    pass

item = SpecialSession.from_minutes(12)
print(item.title, item.minutes)
print(isinstance(item, SpecialSession))
print(Session.valid_minutes(0))
print(Session.valid_minutes(-1))
```
Output:
```text
Study 12
True
True
False
```
SpecialSession inherits the methods and initializer. SpecialSession.from_minutes(12) passes SpecialSession as cls, so the new object is a SpecialSession. isinstance checks this.

Replacing cls("Study", minutes) with Session("Study", minutes) always creates a Session, even when called through SpecialSession. Using cls creates an object of the class used for the call, as long as that class's initializer accepts the supplied arguments.
